newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: James Baker named U.N. envoy for Western Sahara.
newsitem.headline: James Baker named U.N. envoy for Western Sahara.

text.p: Former U.S. Secretary of State James Baker was named on Monday as the personal envoy of U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan for Western Sahara, a North African territory whose future has been a bone of contention since Spain withdrew in 1976.

The United Nations has been trying for years to organise a referendum, originally set for January 1992, to decide whether Western Sahara should be incorporated into Morocco, which controls most of the territory, or become independent, as demanded by the Algerian-backed Polisario guerrilla movement.

A ceasefire, monitored by a small U.N. force, went into effect in September 1991. That largely ended a brush-fire war in the sparsely inhabited territory more than half the size of Spain, which has large phosphate deposits and may also have oil.
But the referendum, as called for in a U.N. peace plan, has been repeatedly postponed because of disagreement between the two sides on who should be eligible to vote.

A spokesman for Annan said Baker would assess whether the U.N. plan could be implemented in its present form, whether adjustments acceptable to the two sides might be possible or whether other ways of resolving the conflict could be found.
"Mr. Baker is a most distinguished statesman. He enjoys a high international reputation and commands universal respect. His appointment has been warmly welcomed by the parties," the spokesman added.

He said Baker expected to visit the region soon for talks with the Moroccan government, the leadership of Polisario and the governments of Algeria and Mauritania, neighbouring countries closely involved in the issue. Polisario's main base is at Tindouf, on the Algerian side of the border with Western Sahara.
Baker was secretary of state under President George Bush from January 1989 to August 1992 and helped rally the U.S.-led coalition that ejected Iraqi troops from Kuwait in 1991.

He was secretary of the treasury from 1985 to 1989 under President Ronald Reagan and served as Reagan's White House chief of staff from 1981 to 1985. He is a senior partner in the law firm of Baker and Botts, with offices in Houston and Washington.

In a statement issued after the announcement of his appointment, Baker said: "I am pleased to do what I can to help resolve this issue, and will explore with the parties all viable options ... I will travel to the area next month for initial contacts with the parties involved."
American U.N. representative Bill Richardson called Baker "a distinguished diplomat with an extensive record of success in international affairs."
"Having worked with him on important foreign policy issues in the past, I am confident that his involvement will provide a significant boost to efforts to resolve the problems in the region."
